Of all the puzzles brought to my friend Sherlock Holmes during our long friendship, only two reached him through me: the affair of Mr. Hatherley’s thumb and that of Colonel Warburton’s madness. The latter perhaps gave greater scope to an acute and original observer. But the former began so strangely and contained such dramatic incidents that it may better deserve a written account, even though it offered fewer opportunities for the deductive reasoning by which Holmes obtained his remarkable results. I believe the newspapers have told the story more than once. Yet, as with all such accounts, its effect is diminished when presented _en bloc_ in half a column of print. It is far more striking when the facts unfold before one’s eyes and each fresh discovery clears another part of the mystery, leading step by step towards the whole truth. The circumstances impressed me deeply at the time. Two years have passed, but that impression has scarcely faded.

The events I am about to recount happened in the summer of 1889, shortly after my marriage. I had returned to civilian medical practice and finally left Holmes alone in his Baker Street rooms. Nevertheless, I visited him frequently and occasionally persuaded him to abandon his Bohemian habits enough to call on us. My practice grew steadily. Living fairly near Paddington Station, I acquired several patients among the railway staff. One, whom I had cured of a painful and persistent illness, never tired of praising my abilities. He tried to send me every sick person over whom he had any influence.

One morning, just before seven, the maid knocked to wake me. Two men from Paddington were waiting in my consulting-room. Experience had taught me that railway cases were rarely minor, so I dressed quickly and hurried downstairs. As I approached, my old ally, the guard, came out and carefully closed the door behind him.
“I’ve brought him,” he whispered, jerking his thumb back over his shoulder. “He’s safely inside.”
“What have you brought?” I asked. His manner suggested he had shut some curious creature in my room.

“A new patient,” he whispered. “Thought I’d bring him myself, so he couldn’t get away. There he is, safe and sound. Must be off now, Doctor. I have my duties, just like you.” And my faithful recruiter departed before I could even thank him.

In the consulting-room I found a gentleman sitting beside the table. He wore a modest suit of heather tweed and had placed a soft cloth cap on my books. Around one of his hands he had wrapped a handkerchief, its surface blotched with blood. He was young—no more than twenty-five, I thought—with a strong, masculine face. But he was extremely pale and seemed deeply agitated, as though controlling his emotions required all his strength of mind.

“I am sorry to wake you so early, Doctor,” he said. “I had a very serious accident during the night. I arrived by train this morning and asked at Paddington where I could find a doctor. A kindly fellow brought me here himself. I gave your maid my card, but I see she left it on the side-table.”

I picked up the card and read it: ‘Mr. Victor Hatherley, hydraulic engineer, 16A Victoria Street, third floor.’ Such were my visitor’s name, profession, and address. “I am sorry to have kept you waiting,” I said, sitting in my library chair. “You have just completed a night journey, I gather, which is a monotonous business in itself.”

“Oh, I could hardly call the night I have just spent monotonous,” he replied, laughing. He leaned back and shook with loud, ringing laughter. Every medical instinct I possessed protested against the sound.
“Stop!” I cried. “Compose yourself!” I poured out some water from a carafe.

It did no good. He had surrendered to one of those hysterical fits that sometimes overcome strong people after a great crisis has passed. Eventually he recovered himself, looking exhausted and very pale.
“I have behaved like a fool,” he gasped.
“Not at all. Drink this.” I added a splash of brandy to the water. Colour began returning to his bloodless cheeks.
“That is better!” he said. “Now, Doctor, would you kindly look at my thumb—or rather, at the place where it used to be?”

He unwound the handkerchief and extended his hand. Even my experienced nerves recoiled at the sight. Four fingers projected above a dreadful red, spongy surface where the thumb should have been. It had been cut or torn away at its base.
“Good heavens!” I exclaimed. “A terrible wound. You must have lost a great deal of blood.”

“Yes. I fainted when it happened and must have remained unconscious for a long time. When I woke, it was still bleeding. I bound one end of my handkerchief tightly around the wrist and used a twig to tighten it.”
“Excellent! You ought to have become a surgeon.”
“It was a hydraulic problem, you see, so it fell within my own field.”
“A very heavy, sharp implement caused this,” I said, examining the wound.
“Something like a cleaver,” he replied.
“An accident, I assume?”
“Certainly not an accident.”
“What! Someone tried to murder you?”
“Most decidedly murderous.”
“That is horrifying.”
I sponged and cleaned the wound, dressed it, then covered it with cotton padding and carbolic bandages. He leaned back without flinching, though occasionally he bit his lip.
“How does that feel?” I asked when I had finished.
“Splendid! Your brandy and bandaging have made a new man of me. I was terribly weak, but then I have endured a great deal.”
“Perhaps you should not discuss it. It is clearly putting a strain on your nerves.”

“Oh, no, not now. I shall have to give my account to the police. Between ourselves, though, if I did not have this wound as convincing evidence, I would be surprised if they believed my statement. It is an extraordinary story, and I have very little proof to support it. Even if they believe me, the clues I can supply are so indefinite that it remains doubtful whether justice will be done.”
“Ah!” I exclaimed. “If there is anything in the nature of a mystery that you wish to see solved, I strongly advise you to consult my friend Sherlock Holmes before approaching the official police.”
“I have heard of him,” my visitor answered. “I would be delighted if he took an interest, though naturally I must also involve the police. Would you be kind enough to introduce me to him?”
“Better still, I shall take you there myself.”
“I would be very much obliged to you.”
“Let us take a cab together. We should arrive in time to share his breakfast. Do you feel strong enough?”
“Yes. I shall not rest until I have told someone.”

“Then my servant will call a cab. I shall join you in a moment.” I hurried upstairs to explain briefly to my wife. Five minutes later I was in a hansom beside my new acquaintance, on our way to Baker Street.

As I expected, Holmes was lounging in his sitting-room in a dressing-gown, reading the personal notices in _The Times_ and smoking his pre-breakfast pipe. Its contents were the tobacco plugs and half-smoked remnants left from the day before, carefully dried and collected at one corner of the mantelpiece. He welcomed us with quiet friendliness, ordered more bacon and eggs, and joined us for a hearty breakfast. Afterwards he settled our visitor on the sofa, put a pillow beneath his head, and left a glass of brandy and water within reach.

“Plainly your experience has been far from ordinary, Mr. Hatherley,” he said. “Lie back and make yourself entirely comfortable. Tell us whatever you can, but stop if you grow tired, and take a little stimulant to maintain your strength.”

“Thank you,” my patient replied. “But I have felt transformed since the doctor dressed my hand, and breakfast has completed the cure. To take as little of your valuable time as possible, I shall begin my strange account at once.”

Holmes settled into his large armchair, wearing the tired, heavy-lidded expression that concealed his keen, eager nature. I sat opposite him. Together we listened without interruption to our visitor’s remarkable story.

“First,” he began, “I am an orphan and unmarried, living alone in London lodgings. I work as a hydraulic engineer. During my seven-year apprenticeship with Venner & Matheson, the well-known Greenwich firm, I gained extensive experience. Two years ago, after completing my apprenticeship and inheriting a reasonable sum on my poor father’s death, I decided to establish my own business. I rented professional rooms in Victoria Street.

“Starting independently in business is probably discouraging for everyone. For me it has been exceptionally so. In two years I have had three consultations and one small commission: nothing else whatsoever. My total receipts amount to twenty-seven pounds ten shillings. Every day I sat in my little office from nine until four, waiting. Finally my spirits began to fail, and I came to believe I would never establish a practice at all.

“Yesterday, however, just as I was preparing to leave, my clerk announced a gentleman who wished to discuss business. He brought a card engraved ‘Colonel Lysander Stark’. The colonel followed close behind him. He was a little taller than the average man, but extraordinarily, almost unbelievably thin. I doubt I have ever seen a thinner man. His face narrowed into a sharp nose and chin, and the skin of his cheeks stretched tightly across projecting bones. Yet he seemed naturally lean rather than ill: his eyes were bright, his step brisk, and his manner confident. His clothes were plain but neat. I judged him nearer forty than thirty.
“‘Mr. Hatherley?’ he asked with a trace of a German accent. ‘You have been recommended to me as a man who combines professional skill with discretion and the ability to keep a secret.’
“I bowed, flattered as any young man would be by such words. ‘May I ask who spoke so highly of me?’
“‘Well, perhaps it would be better if I did not tell you that at this particular moment. The same person informed me that you are an orphan, unmarried, and living alone in London.’

“‘That is entirely correct,’ I replied. ‘But forgive me: I do not see how these facts concern my professional qualifications. I understood you wished to consult me about a matter connected with my profession?’

“‘Certainly. Everything I say is relevant, as you will discover. I have a commission for you, but absolute secrecy is essential—absolute secrecy, you understand. Naturally we can expect that more readily from a man living alone than from one surrounded by a family.’
“‘If I give my word to keep a secret,’ I said, ‘you can rely on it absolutely.’
“While I was speaking, he examined me very closely indeed. I thought I had never encountered eyes so suspicious and searching.
“‘Will you promise, then?’ he asked at last.
“‘Yes. I give you my word.’
